headline: Charles Island Flood Tide: Bass Crash Bunker While Porgies Hold the Rocks
subhead: The new moon push turned the bunker schools inside out this week, and the breakwalls are still stacked with porgies and better-grade sea bass underneath.
body_markdown:
Fifteen-porgy limits off the New Haven Harbor east breakwall have been the story of the week, and the sea bass mixed in with them are running better than they have all summer — solid two-pound fish coming up on green crab and squid strips instead of the dink-sized throwbacks that clogged the June opener. That's not an accident. Water off Kings Point is sitting near 71 degrees and New London's holding around 69, which tells you the Central Sound is riding that comfortable late-summer window where bottom fish stack tight to structure before the real cooldown starts pushing them out. The rockpiles from the harbor jetties out to Stratford Shoal are holding fish, and they're not going anywhere yet.

The bigger story, though, is what happened topside. The new moon on the 10th delivered the hardest tidal push of the young fall season, and it did exactly what we flagged last week it would — bunker schools that had been loosely scattered through the western Sound got squeezed tight against the beaches, the river mouths, and the sandbar off Charles Island, and the stripers finally committed instead of just picking at stragglers. That's the difference between a scattered bite and a real one. Boats working the bar on the last two hours of the flood found bunker balled up so thick the surface went nervous, with bass blowing through from underneath. Live-lined bunker on a stinger rig has been the most consistent producer, but guys throwing big Danny-style swimbaits and white bucktails with a curly-tail trailer are connecting too, especially at first light before the boat traffic pushes the bait deeper.

Structure guys haven't been left out of the striper conversation either. The rockpiles off Falkner Island have been holding fish on the down-tide side, particularly on the last two hours of the ebb when current wraps the island and bait gets pinned against the ledge. Bucktails in the 1.5 to 2-ounce range, dropped and hopped slow off the bottom, have taken slot fish in that 28 to 32-inch range, with the occasional overslot mixed in for boats willing to work the deeper water on the north side.

Back on the bottom, blackfish are starting to show a little more interest as water eases, though it's early yet — the real tautog run doesn't kick until the water drops another five or six degrees. Right now the best action for tog is coming off the rockpiles inside Milford Gulf, where green crabs fished on a simple knocker rig in 15 to 20 feet are picking off a few keepers on the slower stages of the tide, either dead low or right at the top of the flood before current picks up too much to hold bottom cleanly.

Porgies remain the most dependable fish in the zone right now, and that's not a knock — it's the kind of bite you can set a clock by. The breakwalls at New Haven Harbor, the rockpiles off Hammonasset, and the drop-offs around Charles Island are all holding porgies in the 10 to 13-inch range, with bigger fish mixed in on the deeper water outside the wall. Squid strips and clam belly on a high-low rig, fished right on bottom with just enough weight to hold in the current, is still the standard, and there's no reason to get fancy with it.

Fluke are the one piece of this puzzle that's fading fast, and that's playing out exactly like we expected — the keeper-grade fish have largely pulled off the shallow structure and started their move toward deeper, cooler water ahead of the fall exit. What's left inside Milford Gulf and around the harbor flats is mostly short fish, fun on light tackle but not worth targeting specifically anymore. If fluke is still on the must-catch list, the better window closed about two weeks ago.

Looking at the next few days, the moon is easing off its new-moon peak but the tidal energy built into this system doesn't disappear overnight — expect the bunker-driven striper bite to stay active through the weekend, particularly on the Charles Island bar and around the river mouths at first light and last light. If the wind stays out of the northwest and holds under 15 knots, which is the current setup, water clarity should stay clean enough to keep sight-casting to bunker pods a realistic option rather than just blind-casting into churn. Porgies and sea bass should hold steady on the breakwalls and rockpiles regardless of wind direction since they're not chasing bait around, they're just sitting on structure waiting for the tide to bring dinner to them. Blackfish will keep improving gradually as the water eases through the 60s over the next couple weeks, so it's worth scouting the deeper rockpiles now even if the bite isn't fully switched on yet. The best single piece of advice for anyone with limited time this weekend: fish the last two hours of the flood at Charles Island for bass, then slide over to the breakwall on the dropping tide for a bucket of porgies and a shot at a keeper sea bass. That combination is producing right now, and there's no strong reason to think it stops soon.
